We have something special planned for our September meeting as we celebrate the 20th anniversary of the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild. Among a few other special activities
planned, we will take a few moments to reflect back on the history of the Guild and its founders, enjoy some especially tasty treats and be entertained to a highly engaging presentation
by Larry Stevenson entitled “A Box With a Twist”. Be sure to come out and help celebrate
our 20th year!
I hope everyone had a great summer and were able to enjoy many of the wonderful things
this beautiful corner of the world has to offer. Of course, one of the highlights of our summer
was the annual GVWG BBQ and Tool Swap. Once again it was planned, organized and graciously hosted by Dan and Yolanda Breck in their gorgeous and spacious back yard. Between
the burgers and dogs provided by the Guild and the many scrumptious appies and desserts
brought by the members, there was certainly no shortage of food and conversation.
I also hope you were able to squeeze in some time at the lathe and hopefully began learning a
new skill. If you recall, the President’s Challenge for the September meeting was to spend
the summer learning something new. To that end, when we weren’t at the cottage or enjoying all our various summer activities, I managed to squeeze in some time online and in my
shop learning about and experimenting with some of the many methods of texturing and colouring wood using various types of power-carving tools and water-based dyes or acrylic
paints. Like most things, the more I learned the more I discovered I needed or wanted to
learn so it’s an ongoing process with a lot more to discover and experiment with. Most importantly, I’m having a ton of fun! As you are no doubt aware, YouTube is a fantastic tool for
learning and discovering, although you sometimes have to take some of the information with
a healthy dose of caution or skepticism. I found that picking the brains of other turners who
are far more knowledgeable and experienced than I was most invaluable. It never ceases to
amaze me how our members are so willing to spend time sharing their knowledge and experience. As an extra bonus long the way, I discovered a whole host of new tools, tooling and
art supplies that I needed to acquire. Mmmm… More tools…
In addition to our usual Instant Gallery display we would like to ask and encourage members
to bring in their very first turning or a very early work along with something more current to
show off beside it. It will be a great way to see how far your skills and interests have progressed and help encourage our newer turners as they pursue their own woodturning paths.
Don’t forget to bring something for the President’s Challenge: What I Learned This Summer.
It doesn’t need to be a finished piece; bring along some of your experiments, samples or any

Editor's Notes
In celebration of our 20th season of the GVWG I look back at the Newsletter editors/publishers that have
preceded me.
The newsletter began as soon as the Guild started meeting in September 1999. Our first editor was Amie
Hillaby. She enthusiastically took on the role of recording Guild activities and providing us with notices
of upcoming events. It is striking to recall that we kept the newsletter short because they needed to be
printed and mailed to many members who did not yet have email. Also, electronic publishing was in its
infancy so colour, embedded pictures and layout templates would not come along for some time.
Since the start 16 people have worked, either individually or as editor/publisher teams, to keep our
newsletter going. In 20 years they missed just one scheduled edition. Knowing the time and effort
needed to pull issues together I think that is an outstanding achievement.
Here are the folks that have delivered your newsletter over the last 20 years.
Do you have Guild stories from the last 20 years? Send them to us and we will include them in this year
of celebration. Send then to editor@gvwg.ca
Bruce Campbell Robert Carlson

Ringing the Bell: Celebrating important milestones for cancer patients
At BC Cancer patients “Ring the Bell” to celebrate important milestones in what is often a
long and difficult journey for all involved. BC Cancer – Surrey recently set up a Milestone
Bell for patients and families who can choose to “ring the bell” at any moment through
their course of treatment. The bell is stationed at the bottom of the stairs on Level 1 at the
Radiation Therapy Department at the Surrey Centre and is not only there to help patients
to celebrate milestones, but the sound of it reminds the staff why we are here.
Radiation therapists Julie Nager and Katie Katie Chartrand played an important role in
leading this initiative of the Milestone Bell. They began by contacting patient and family
partners to ask them for ideas and feedback. Then they started searching for a bell. The
Bull family who has roots in the navy, kindly donated their grandfather’s bell; a former
patient at BC Cancer – Surrey. Next they went searching for a plaque. The wood was
found and turned by Greater Vancouver Woodturner Guild (GVWG) member Phil Vetra,
himself cancer survivor who was treated at the Centre. GVWG member Steve Fairbarin,
donated the laser engraving on the plaque.
Canada 150 Tree gets a permanent home
In addition to our new bell, the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild presented us a
beautiful hand-carved tree that we proudly display in the Radiation Therapy Department. 25 members of their group designed and crafted the tree to celebrate Canada’s
150th. They sincerely hope that this permanent installation will bring joy and uplift the

The fall Turning 101 course will be held over
the last weekend in October (Sat 26th & Sun
27th) and first Saturday in November (Sat 2nd)
and is open to all GVWG members. Bruce
Campbell has again generously volunteered his
time as lead instructor and will share his
wealth of woodturning knowledge and experience.
For those new to woodturning, Turning 101 is
a great way to become familiar with woodturning tools, techniques, and safe practices. The
course covers both spindle and bowl turning
with an emphasis on safety. You will do LOTS
of turning over the 3 days and by the end you
should have enough knowledge to confidently
purchase equipment and turn in your own
shop safely.
That said, Turning 101 is not just for new
members. It can provide an excellent refresher
on woodturning basics and is a great opportunity to refresh your skills and expand your
knowledge.
If you do not have tools please DO NOT purchase them beforehand. You will be lent tools
during the class. However, if you have tools
already then please bring them with you.
The cost is $150 and covers 3 days of instruction, use of an individual lathe and tools, all
wood and other consumables. The course will
the held at the KMS Tools Workshop, 110
Woolridge St in Coquitlam and is limited to 6
people. Registration is on a first come basis,
with confirmation upon receipt of the course
fees. For more information and to register
please email peterhill64@telus.net
Announcing Turning 101

to be held Sept. 27 – Oct. 6, 2019 Calgary

If you have an interest in fine woodworking then
mark your calendar for the Southern Alberta
Woodworkers Society (SAWS) “Fine Works in
Wood Exhibition and Sale” Sept. 27 to Oct. 6,
2019. It takes place in the Center Court of Southcentre Mall, Calgary, Alta. during regular mall
hours. There is no admittance charge.
Pieces on display (and for sale) cover a broad
range from functional to artistic, furniture to fine
wood turnings and purely artwork, says spokesman Neil Dorin. “This venue allows people to get
close to the displays so they can closely examine
the workmanship.”
“Woodworking is growing.” says Dorin. “The exhibition is a celebration of the very best work of our
members and the exhibit area will be staffed by
SAWS members who can help to answer your
questions.”
SAWS was established 35 years ago as a way to
bring the woodworking community together in a
social and learning environment. SAWS membership is open to anyone. Regular meetings feature
speakers, tours of woodworking establishments
and tours of local member’s shops and projects.
Information about the Southern Alberta Woodworking Society may be found at the organization’s website www.saws.ca.

 Always wear safety goggles or safety glasses that
include side protectors. Use a full face shield for
bowl, vessel, or any turning involving chucks and
faceplates.
 Use a combination of dust mask, air filtration helmet, proper ventilation, and/or dust collection system as appropriate. Fine particles from a grinder
and wood dust are harmful to your respiratory system.
 Wear hearing protection during extended periods
of turning.
 Turn the lathe off before adjusting the tool rest or
tool rest base, i.e., banjo.
 Always remove chuck keys, adjusting wrenches,
and knockout bars immediately after use. Never
leave them in place, even for a moment.
 Tie back long hair and avoid loose clothing, jewelry,
or any dangling objects that may catch on rotating
parts or accessories.
 When using a faceplate, be certain the workpiece is
solidly mounted with stout screws (#10 or #12
sheet metal screws as a minimum). Do not use dry
wall or deck screws.
 When turning between centers, be certain the
workpiece is firmly mounted between the headstock driving center and tailstock center.
 Ensure the belt guard or cover is in place.
 Check that all locking devices on the tailstock and
tool rest assembly (rest and base) are tight before
operating the lathe.
 Ensure the blank is securely fastened.
 Rotate your workpiece backwards by hand to make
sure it clears the toolrest and bed before turning
the lathe on.
 Stay clear of the areas directly behind and in front
of the workpiece, they are the most likely areas for
a piece to travel as it comes off the lathe. A good
safety habit is to step out of this zone when turning
on the lathe, keeping your hand on the switch in
case you need to turn the machine off. When observing someone else turn, stay out of these zones.
 Always check the speed of the lathe before turning
it on. Use slower speeds for larger diameters or
rough pieces and higher speeds for smaller diameters and pieces that are balanced. Always start a
piece at a slower speed until the workpiece is balanced. If the lathe is shaking or vibrating, lower the
speed. If the workpiece vibrates, always stop the
machine to verify why. As a starting point, consult
your operator’s manual for recommended speeds
for a particular lathe. Ensure the lathe speed is
compatible with the size of the blank.
 Exercise extra caution when using stock with
cracks, splits, checks, bark pockets, knots, irregular
shapes, or protuberances. Beginners should avoid
these types of stock until they have greater
knowledge of working such wood.
 Hold turning tools securely on the toolrest, holding
the tool in a controlled but comfortable manner.
Always contact the tool rest with the tool before
contacting the wood.
 Note that, when running a lathe in reverse, it is
possible for a chuck or faceplate to unscrew unless
it is securely tightened or locked on the lathe spindle.
 Know your capabilities and limitations. An experienced woodturner is capable of lathe speeds, techniques, and procedures not recommended for beginning turners.
 Always remove the tool rest before sanding, finishing, or polishing operations.
 Don’t overreach, keep proper footing, and keep
your balance at all times.
 Keep your lathe in good repair. Check for damaged
parts, alignment, binding of moving parts, and other conditions that may affect its operation.
 Keep tools sharp and clean for better and safer perYou mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning

Page 18
GVWG
formance. Don’t force a dull tool. Don’t use a tool
for a purpose for which it was not designed or intended.
 Consider your work environment. Don’t use a
lathe in damp or wet locations. Do not use in presence of inflammable liquids or gases, and always
keep a fully-charged fire extinguisher close at
hand. Keep your work area well lit.
 Stay alert. Watch what you are doing. Pay close
attention to unusual sounds or vibrations. Stop
the lathe to investigate the cause. Don’t operate
machines when you are tired or under the influence of drugs or alcohol.
 Guard against electric shock. Inspect electric
cords for damage. Avoid the use of extension
cords.
 Never leave the lathe running unattended. Turn
power off. Don’t leave lathe until it comes to a
complete stop.
 Many accidents to woodturners occur while using
saws, especially band and chain saws. Learn and
follow the safety guidelines for this equipment.
You mostly turn alone so safety is YOUR responsibility.
Safety Guidelines for Wood Turning
